title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n\operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
formal:
Do there exist absolute real constants \(C\geq1\), \(K>0\), \(d\geq0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\geq3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and all explicitly given \(x,y\in\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}^n\), every execution uses at most
\[Kn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\]
word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq C\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The constants and program are chosen once for all input lengths and all pairs. The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance; the probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness on that fixed pair.
definitions:
Write \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input is \(n\geq1\) followed by two arrays of \(n\) symbols from \(\Sigma_n\), stored in consecutive memory cells with one symbol per word. Binary strings and strings over any fixed alphabet are included after relabeling. The arrays are explicitly present; there is no compressed representation, access oracle, preprocessed database or promised input distribution.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Inserted and substituted symbols belong to \(\Sigma_n\), and intermediate strings may have any finite length. Each operation has cost one; leaving an equal symbol unchanged has cost zero. No transpositions, block moves, variable symbol weights or affine gap penalties are allowed. A substitution costs one, not two. The optimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with one fixed integer \(B\geq3\) for the algorithm. A word represents an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\); memory addresses are words and all cells outside the given input are initially zero. The machine has a fixed finite instruction sequence and fixed integer constants, independent of \(n,x,y\). The unit-cost instructions are random-access reads or writes of one word, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. Shifts fill with zeros and discard overflow; a shift amount at least \(w\) gives zero. Address calculations obey the same costs. Larger integers occupy several words and require several charged instructions. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, advice, oracle or quantum instruction is available.

One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; its individual bits are independent fair bits, and different draws are independent. All preprocessing, memory operations, random draws and output writing count toward the bound. The output is an integer in signed binary notation. Only its value is requested, not a sequence of edits. Every execution must terminate within the stated bound, including those that produce an incorrect estimate. An incorrect execution may return an integer outside the interval. The success guarantee is separate for every pair, not an average over an input distribution.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,d,B,A\;\forall n,x,y\), followed by the displayed probability and all-execution time requirements. Neither the approximation factor nor the logarithmic exponent may grow with \(n\). There is no promise that the distance is large or positive. In particular, when \(x=y\), successful output must be zero. There is no additive error. The shorthand \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) refers exactly to one bound of the displayed form with fixed \(K,d\), not to \(n^{1+\eta}\) for each fixed \(\eta>0\) or to an arbitrary \(n^{1+o(1)}\) overhead.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants meeting both requirements on all input pairs, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every finite approximation constant, every fixed logarithmic exponent and every permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant; failure at one chosen factor or for deterministic algorithms alone is insufficient. A conditional lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. An \(n^{1+\eta}\)-time algorithm for a fixed positive \(\eta\), an approximation factor growing with input length, an additive-error guarantee, an expected-time bound alone, or a theorem only for distant pairs does not settle the question. A large but fixed approximation constant is acceptable. This is an existence question, with no additional numerical approximation tolerance on its answer.
why: This asks whether allowing one universal constant loss of alignment accuracy reduces worst-case sequence comparison to the cost of reading the input, apart from a fixed polylogarithmic overhead. The result would locate a basic computational boundary that remains beyond the known fast constant-factor algorithms. Even a large universal factor would resolve this existence question.

importance.reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.

progress.text: Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial-factor approximation in almost-linear time; the full preprint is dated 26 September 2011 and records a STOC 2009 precursor.
Backurs–Indyk establish conditional hardness for strongly subquadratic exact edit distance.
The revised Koucký–Saks theorem gives a fast constant factor on distant pairs and an additive term in its guarantee on general inputs.
Andoni–Nosatzki announce constant approximation for all pairs with each fixed positive runtime slack; the checked full revision is from July 2022.
Mao–Rubinstein announce near-exact approximation with a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time, subsequently published at STOC 2026.
The Andoni–Nosatzki journal article is published online; its fixed-slack runtime does not become a fixed polylogarithmic overhead.

status_note: The checked Andoni–Nosatzki full theorem and August 2026 journal abstract retain fixed positive runtime slack and a factor depending on that slack. Mao–Rubinstein’s 2026 scheme has a different runtime, while the older far-pair and subpolynomial results have weaker approximation guarantees. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full solution of the saved fixed-factor, fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead target. Full cited proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These user-approved targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.

sentences: Edit distance is the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming one string into another.
The question asks for one randomized algorithm with a universal constant approximation factor and only a fixed polylogarithmic overhead beyond linear input length.
Its runtime must hold on every execution and its probability of a correct multiplicative estimate must be at least two thirds separately on every pair.
Known fixed-slack constant-factor algorithms and earlier subpolynomial or additive approximations do not meet all these requirements simultaneously.
The target remains distinct from the two retained questions about arbitrarily accurate estimates at slower stated runtimes.
